title: Om, from throat to lips
hook: why Nani starts every prayer with om, and a sound that walks across the mouth
carry: om: the one sound for brahman
tomorrow: how can one puff of breath turn a hand into something harsh?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesha as Vyasa's scribe, and a line: holy words are honored, and understood first. Today, the holiest sound of all, and the map of the mouth it walks across.

Open wide and say ahh, the way a doctor asks. That sound comes from the very back, the throat. Now close your lips and hum. The front. Sanskrit lays out its letters exactly that way, throat first, lips last: a map of the mouth. And there's one sound Hindus say before almost every prayer that walks the whole map in a single breath: om.
screen: `SAY AHH: THE THROAT.` → `HUM: THE LIPS.` → `ONE SOUND WALKS THE WHOLE MAP.`

segments.voice: In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa waits three nights at the house of Death, unfed. When Yama, the lord of death, comes home, he offers the boy three wishes to make up for it. For the last one, Nachiketa asks what nothing else can buy: what happens after death, and what lasts. Yama tries to talk him out of it. Take wealth, he says, long life, sons and grandsons, every pleasure. The boy turns them all down. So Yama teaches him, and partway through he names the word that all the Vedas point toward: om. That syllable, Yama says, is Brahman, the reality behind everything. Another Upanishad, the Mandukya, hears om as three sounds, a, u and m, and the silence after. Feel it in your mouth. The a opens at the throat. The u rounds the lips. The m closes them. Throat to lips, the same road the alphabet takes, so many teachers read om as holding all of speech in one syllable. The Mandukya matches a, u and m to waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after to the Self beyond all three. That's why a puja, a prayer, a recitation of the Gita so often opens with om, and why a family chant can close om shanti shanti shanti. Before any words, the one sound that, the Upanishads say, points to everything.
screen: `NACHIKETA AT DEATH'S DOOR.` · `THE WORD ALL THE VEDAS POINT TO: OM.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE AFTER.` · `THROAT, LIPS, CLOSED.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and breathe in. On the out-breath, chant om slowly, the way Hindus do before prayer: let the a open at the back of the throat, the u round the lips, the m close them into a hum you can feel in your face. Then rest in the quiet after, the part the Mandukya calls the fourth. Do it a few times. If you'd rather not chant, just hum, and feel the sound travel forward.
The sounds: Sanskrit's letters laid out from throat to lips, and om, which walks that road in one breath.
Keep this: om, the one sound for Brahman, walking from the throat to the lips. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Om is chanted at the start (and often the end) of Hindu prayers, pujas and recitations; the Mandukya Upanishad treats it as a, u, m and a silent fourth. Sanskrit's consonants are traditionally recited row by row, from the throat to the lips.

notes: Answers 1438's question. First day of 'the sounds'. Taittiriya 1.2 lists varṇa, svara, mātrā, bala, sāma, santāna; the voice paraphrases five of them ('the sound, its pitch, its length, its effort, and how sounds join') and leaves sāma unnamed. Confirm.
Ashtadhyayi 1.1.9 tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam, paraphrased. The five consonant rows (velar, palatal, retroflex, dental, labial) are standard; the voice names them in plain English.
Karmaṇi's ṇ is retroflex (ण). Day 1447 (another writer) covers vowel length; this day stays on place of articulation. Senses shape: the practice is physical (feeling the place move).
